title: Rust 1.99: upgrade your project without guessing
summary: A practical upgrade guide: separate compiler releases from editions and dependencies, establish a baseline, test the targets you actually ship, and know what Rust 1.99 changes.

sections.heading: Start with the problem you want to solve
paragraphs: A compiler upgrade is easier to evaluate when it answers a concrete question. Perhaps a dependency needs a newer compiler. Perhaps a diagnostic could help a teammate understand a failure. Perhaps you want to stay on the supported stable release. Write that reason down before changing files. It will help you distinguish a successful upgrade from an unrelated refactor that happened during the same afternoon.

As of 10 October 2026, Rust 1.99.0 is the current stable release, announced on 1 October. This article uses that version as the destination for an existing project. The process is deliberately small: record a baseline, select the new toolchain, run meaningful checks, investigate differences, and keep evidence. You can repeat those steps for the next release without inventing a fresh upgrade ritual.

image.alt: A crab checks test cards in a workshop connecting an older tool cabinet to a new one.
image.caption: An upgrade is a maintenance task: keep the old baseline, check the new result, and record what changed.

sections.heading: What the release actually changes
paragraphs: Rust 1.99 stabilises defining C-ABI variadic functions, alongside APIs for inspecting layout through raw pointers and additional standard-library operations. The release also revises guidance for leaking and later reclaiming allocations: code intending to recover ownership should use an ownership-transfer API rather than treating a leaked reference as a temporary detour. These are relevant changes for low-level libraries, but they are not an instruction to add unsafe code to an ordinary application.

For a learning project, the useful first question is whether any change touches your source or dependencies. A command-line parser using owned strings does not automatically need a C variadic function. Make a short impact note: affected directly, affected through a dependency, or no known direct effect. Then test that note. This keeps a release announcement from turning into a shopping list of features your project does not need.

sections.heading: Compiler, edition and dependencies are separate decisions
paragraphs: Updating the compiler does not itself rewrite the edition declared in your package. The edition controls language compatibility choices for that package; the compiler version selects the toolchain that builds it. Dependency requirements and the resolved dependency graph are another concern. Put all three on separate lines in your upgrade note. If you change them together, a new error can have several plausible causes before you have even read it.

For the first pass, keep the existing edition and dependency lockfile. Use the new compiler against the source graph you already understand. If an edition migration is also valuable, do it as a later change with its own checks. The Edition Guide describes migration tooling such as `cargo fix --edition`, but automatic source edits still deserve review. For example, review generated fixes in a small function before accepting them across a large workspace.

image.alt: Five upgrade steps: baseline, pin toolchain, build and test, check targets, record results. Compiler, edition and dependencies are separate choices.
image.caption: Hold the edition and dependency graph steady while checking the compiler upgrade. Migrate them separately when needed.

sections.heading: Make a baseline you can compare
paragraphs: Before switching toolchains, run the project in the way a person uses it. For a small text analyser, keep three fixtures: normal input, empty input, and malformed input. Save the expected output and exit status for each. Also record the compiler version and the exact commands you used. A screenshot of a green terminal is less useful than a reproducible command and a fixture that demonstrates the behaviour you care about.

Keep the baseline narrow enough to repeat. If the application is supposed to count Unicode characters, include a word containing a multibyte character. If it rejects negative quantities, include a negative quantity. These checks belong to the product contract, so they remain meaningful even when implementation details change. If the baseline already fails, investigate that failure before describing a later failure as an upgrade regression. You need a known starting point to make that claim.
sections.code:
rustc --version --verbose
cargo test --locked
cargo run --locked -- fixtures/normal.txt
cargo run --locked -- fixtures/empty.txt

sections.heading: Pin the destination and keep the dependency graph stable
paragraphs: For a desktop project managed by rustup, install the destination toolchain and invoke it explicitly. This lets you compare old and new compilers without changing the default for unrelated projects. Once the upgrade is accepted, a project toolchain file can communicate the chosen version to other contributors. Record any required targets or components as part of that environment, rather than expecting every machine to have the same global setup.

The manifest describes dependency requirements, while `Cargo.lock` records a resolved set of versions and sources. Keep that lockfile during the initial comparison. `--locked` asks Cargo to reject a build that would need to change it; it does not promise that every platform-specific input is identical. If the upgrade requires a dependency adjustment, make that adjustment visible and explain why. A reviewable two-file change is easier to reason about than a mysterious regenerated dependency graph.
sections.code:
rustup toolchain install 1.99.0
cargo +1.99.0 test --locked
cargo +1.99.0 check --locked

sections.heading: Run checks that answer different questions
paragraphs: A successful check tells you that the selected source can be type-checked under the selected configuration. Tests tell you what your assertions exercised. A real application run tells you whether its entry point, input handling and output fit together. Treat those as different pieces of evidence. For the text analyser, a unit test of the counting function is useful, but it does not prove that a filename with spaces is handled correctly by the command-line interface.

Choose a small verification table with a question beside every command. Does the library still build? Do examples still compile? Does invalid input produce the intended error? Does the shipping target still work? If a command has no clear question, it may be adding noise. Conversely, if an important behaviour has no evidence, add a check for that behaviour. The goal is a persuasive upgrade record, not the longest possible command transcript.
sections.code:
cargo +1.99.0 check --all-targets --locked
cargo +1.99.0 test --locked
cargo +1.99.0 test --doc --locked
cargo +1.99.0 fmt --check

sections.heading: Investigate a difference before changing the code
paragraphs: Suppose the new compiler reports a warning in a helper function. Read its location and explanation, then isolate the smallest relevant expression. Ask whether the source has a real ambiguity, whether a lint changed, or whether a dependency exposes the warning. Do not immediately suppress it across the entire crate. A local explanation gives future readers something they can evaluate; a blanket allowance removes information from places you have not inspected.

For a changed runtime result, compare the same fixture under both toolchains. Remove unrelated formatting edits from the comparison. If the difference survives in a small example, you now have something useful for a bug report or a dependency issue. If it disappears when you restore the lockfile, the compiler was probably not the only variable. Write the observed condition precisely: which target, which input, which command and which result differed. That precision saves repeated guesswork.

sections.heading: Decide what your minimum supported Rust version means
paragraphs: An application can choose to build with a recent pinned compiler while a library may support older consumers. The `rust-version` manifest field communicates the minimum supported toolchain for a package. Using a newly stabilised API can raise that minimum even if the overall design has not changed. If your package advertises an older version, actually test the supported configuration before publishing an upgrade that relies on a new feature.

Write the support decision for your audience. A private learning tool might simply require the selected release. A reusable library may need to preserve an older minimum until its users can update. Avoid treating the version field as decoration: it is a statement other people use when selecting dependencies. Keep the policy short enough to follow, and separate a minimum-version increase from a compiler maintenance update in your release notes.

sections.heading: Check the platform you ship, including Crabrix
paragraphs: A successful desktop build is evidence for that desktop environment. It does not establish that a WebAssembly target, a phone sandbox or a different operating system behaves identically. Keep platform checks tied to actual requirements: filesystem paths, available imports, memory limits and package build requirements. A dependency can compile on your laptop and still require capabilities that an on-device environment does not provide. Target compatibility is a separate part of the upgrade decision.

Crabrix bundles its compiler in the application. Reading a new Rust release article does not update that bundled compiler, and a website account does not change it either. Check the compiler and target shown by your installed app. Use the app for examples supported by that environment, and validate desktop release-specific experiments on the corresponding desktop toolchain. This distinction makes lesson results easier to interpret and prevents a new language feature from looking like an unexplained editor failure.

sections.heading: Treat performance as an experiment
paragraphs: A compiler upgrade may change build time or runtime performance, but a single stopwatch reading is a weak comparison. Start by naming the workload. For the text analyser, choose a fixed input file, the same output mode and the same build profile. Record whether the build cache is warm or cold. A faster cached build and a slower clean build can both be true, because they measure different work. Keep those conditions beside the results so a teammate can reproduce the comparison.

Run the selected workload several times under comparable conditions and check its output each time. A programme that finishes faster because it skips a required operation has not improved the task you meant to measure. Separate an observation from an explanation: this command took less time is an observation; this optimiser change caused it is a hypothesis that needs more evidence. If the difference is too small or inconsistent to distinguish from normal variation, say that. You can accept an upgrade for compatibility or maintenance reasons without claiming a performance benefit you have not established.

sections.heading: Keep a short acceptance record
paragraphs: Finish with a record another developer can use tomorrow. State the old and new compiler versions, the retained edition, whether the lockfile changed, the targets checked, the fixtures run and any remaining limitation. Include the reason for the upgrade from the first section. If a check was skipped because the target was unavailable, say so directly. An honest gap is more useful than a broad claim that everything is compatible.

For your next practice session, take a small existing Rust project and write the baseline before touching its configuration. Then change only the compiler selection and rerun the same commands. Explain one result in plain language: what did that check prove, and what did it leave untested? That habit scales from a five-line lesson to a maintained application. New releases become manageable changes when you can connect each decision to a concrete observation.

title: Ownership in a real Rust program: choose who keeps the data
summary: Build a tiny message workflow to understand moves, shared borrows, mutable borrows and cloning. Learn to choose function signatures from the job they do.

sections.heading: Give ownership a concrete job
paragraphs: Imagine a small program that receives a message, counts its characters, appends a note, and produces a final report. The message is ordinary text stored in a `String`. Several functions need access to it, but they do not all need the same kind of access. Counting reads. Appending changes. Producing the final report may take responsibility for the original text. That difference is where ownership becomes useful in everyday design.

Before writing signatures, describe what each function promises its caller. Does the caller still need the message afterwards? Should the function be able to change it? Does the function need to keep it after returning? Those questions are easier to answer than a vague question about satisfying the borrow checker. We will use one message throughout this article and change one decision at a time, so you can predict the effect of each signature.

image.alt: A crab passes a single message card between reading, editing and final-report stations.
image.caption: Reading a message, editing it, and taking it into a report are three different jobs.

sections.heading: Start with one owner
paragraphs: Create `let message = String::from("hello");`. The binding named `message` owns this `String` value. The string manages its text storage, and dropping the owned value releases that storage. Think of the owner as the place responsible for the value's lifetime, rather than a label attached permanently to one physical address. The compiler follows how responsibility moves through your program.

For this example, write a tiny ownership ledger beside the source. Before a function call, the caller owns the message. During the call, note whether ownership transfers or the function only receives a reference. After the call, mark which value remains available. The ledger is not code and does not need a sophisticated diagram. Three lines on paper can reveal why a later use is valid, or why it attempts to use a value that has already moved.

sections.heading: A move transfers responsibility
paragraphs: Suppose `into_report` accepts a `String` and returns a newly formatted `String`. Calling `into_report(message)` transfers the argument into the function. The caller cannot continue using the moved binding afterwards. This is often a useful API: the caller has finished working with the original message, and the function is explicitly responsible for turning it into the final representation.

The returned report is a value with a new owner in the caller. Our ledger therefore changes from caller owns message, to function owns message, to caller owns report. The exact internal implementation may allocate a new buffer, reuse storage, or combine values; the ownership contract tells us which values can be used at each point. Avoid imagining that every move means copying all the text bytes. Responsibility and copying are different questions.

sections.heading: Borrow for the reading job
paragraphs: Counting characters does not need to own the message. Give that function a `&str`: a borrowed view of text. The caller keeps ownership, and the function reads through the view for the duration of the call. `character_count(&message)` works because the owned string can be borrowed as a string slice. The signature also accepts a string literal, so callers are not forced to construct an owned string just to ask a read-only question.

Our reading operation counts Unicode scalar values with `chars().count()`. That is deliberately more specific than counting visible characters: some displayed characters consist of several scalar values. `String::len()` measures bytes, which answers another question. Choose the measurement your program actually needs and name it accurately. Ownership does not settle that product decision for you. A program can be memory-safe and still count the wrong thing if its contract is unclear.

sections.heading: Borrow mutably for the editing job
paragraphs: Appending a note changes the caller's string, so `append_note` takes `&mut String`. The caller must have a mutable binding and must pass a mutable reference. The function can update the value without taking it away. This makes the effect visible in the signature: someone reading the call sees that this operation may change the message they still own.

While a mutable borrow is active, it provides exclusive access to the borrowed value under Rust's borrowing rules. You cannot also use an overlapping shared reference in a way that conflicts with that access. Organise the work into phases: inspect, finish inspecting, then edit. The compiler tracks when references are used; the relevant borrow can end before the surrounding block ends. Small sequential phases usually express the intended workflow more clearly than a tangle of references kept alive unnecessarily.

image.alt: Three separate choices: move ownership into a function, borrow text for reading, or borrow a string mutably for exclusive editing.
image.caption: These are alternatives for a function's job. Shared and mutable access are not shown as simultaneous borrows.

sections.heading: Combine the jobs in a readable order
paragraphs: Now combine the three operations. Count the text while borrowing it, append the note with a mutable borrow, then move the finished message into the report. At every stage, ask who owns the current value and which access is active. The caller keeps the string during the first two jobs and deliberately gives it up for the last. That is a complete ownership story with no extra clone.

Try changing the order before changing the signatures. If you produce the report first and then attempt to count the original binding, you will encounter a moved-value error. That error reflects the contract you selected. Decide whether the programme really needs the original message later, or whether the count should simply happen earlier. A change in operation order may solve the actual design problem more cleanly than adding another allocation.

sections.heading: Use clone when you want independent ownership
paragraphs: Sometimes the application really needs two independently owned strings. Perhaps you must preserve the original user input while building an editable draft. In that case, cloning the string can express a deliberate requirement. Name the values according to their roles: `original` and `draft`. A reader can then see why two owned copies exist and why later edits to the draft should not alter the original.

Cloning is type-specific. For a `String`, it creates an independently owned copy of the text; for other types, the behaviour and cost depend on their `Clone` implementation. Do not apply a universal rule that cloning is always wrong or always cheap. Instead, explain the independence you need. If a function only reads, borrowing may be enough. If two parts need separate ownership and independent changes, a clone may be a reasonable part of the design.

sections.heading: Returning a view ties the result to its source
paragraphs: A function can return a borrowed part of the caller's text. Our `first_word` function takes a `&str` and returns a `&str` selected from it. With this signature, the lifetime elision rules connect the returned reference to the input reference. The caller must keep the underlying text valid for as long as it uses that returned view. The function does not create a new owned copy of the word.

This choice is useful when inspecting a message briefly. If you instead need to save the word independently while discarding or changing the source, an owned result may be the clearer contract. Practise both versions and write down what changes in the ledger. The borrowed version depends on source storage; an owned string has its own ownership story. Neither version is universally better. The requirement to keep or modify the source determines which contract fits.

sections.heading: Read an error as a trace through your program
paragraphs: When the borrow checker rejects a change, locate the places it identifies: where the value moved or a borrow began, and where the conflicting use occurs. Annotate those source lines with your ledger. If you cannot describe the sequence, reduce the example until you can. Keep the same relationship between owner and references while removing unrelated printing, parsing or collection code.

Then propose a change in ordinary language before editing Rust. I need the reading phase to finish before mutation. I need this function to borrow because the caller still uses the value. I need an owned result because its source will disappear. Each statement leads to a specific code change. This habit turns diagnostics into design feedback. Randomly inserting `clone`, `mut` or lifetime parameters can make the compiler quieter without making your data flow easier to understand.

sections.heading: Small numbers have a different contract
paragraphs: If you pass the character count into another function, you may notice that the count remains usable afterwards. That is because a simple integer type such as usize implements Copy. Passing that value can copy it without the explicit ownership transfer behaviour you observed for String. This does not make the message example inconsistent; different types provide different capabilities. Read the type before applying a rule learned from one particular value.

Add a helper that prints the count and then use the count again in the caller. Compare its signature with the function that consumes the message. Write two ledger entries: one for the integer copy, one for the string move. The exercise prevents a common overgeneralisation that every ordinary assignment or argument makes the previous binding unusable. Your model should describe what the selected type permits. When a type does not implement Copy, make the ownership decision explicit through moving, borrowing or a deliberate clone.

sections.heading: A practice exercise with a clear finish
paragraphs: Build a message workflow in Crabrix or on your desktop. Begin with the combined example above. Add a second read-only function that reports whether the message contains a question mark. Call it before appending the note. Then preserve an original string and create a separate draft that receives the note. Explain why the second version needs independent ownership, and compare the output of original, draft and final report.

Finally, return the first word as a borrowed view and deliberately attempt a conflicting edit before using the view. Read the diagnostic, then reorganise the work so the view is consumed before mutation. Your finish condition is not merely a green build: describe every move and borrow in the successful programme, identify the storage behind each view, and explain any clone you retained. Once that explanation is straightforward, ownership has become a tool you can use rather than a rule you are trying to evade.

title: Rust errors that help: design a Result your caller can use
summary: Build a small quantity parser with useful errors, propagate failures without losing their meaning, and turn failure cases into tests and readable output.

sections.heading: Begin with the person receiving the error
paragraphs: A programme that accepts user input will meet values it cannot use. Someone submits an empty quantity, types a word where a number belongs, or requests more than the allowed amount. Those failures are part of the normal interface. A useful error tells the caller what happened and leaves room for an appropriate response: ask for another value, skip a record, show a message, or stop the operation with a clear status.

In this article we will parse the quantity for a small workshop order. The quantity must be an integer from one to one hundred. Our goal is more precise than removing every `unwrap`: we want each expected failure to have a name, every successful value to satisfy the contract, and the programme boundary to explain a failure without exposing irrelevant internals. You can build the example in Crabrix using only the standard library and then adapt the same design to a file or command-line tool.

image.alt: A crab at an input workshop sends a valid order along a mint route and a rejected order to a helpful repair station.
image.caption: Expected input failures need a useful route back to the caller, not an unexplained crash.

sections.heading: Result makes two outcomes explicit
paragraphs: A `Result<T, E>` contains either `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)`. For our parser, the successful value is a `u32`, and the error type describes why no accepted quantity was produced. The type forces a caller to account for the two possibilities when it wants to obtain the success value. Returning an error does not by itself print anything, close a window, or retry a request. Those are decisions made by the caller.

Keep the success contract as important as the failure contract. If the function returns `Ok(7)`, the caller should know that seven satisfied the parser's documented range. It should not need to repeat the same range check just to trust the result. Think of the function as a boundary between raw input and a value the next stage can use. That boundary becomes easier to maintain when success and failure both have a clear meaning.

sections.heading: Name the failures your caller cares about
paragraphs: Our workshop distinguishes missing input, input that cannot be parsed as `u32`, and a parsed quantity outside the allowed range. Those categories correspond to different user guidance. Empty input suggests entering a value. An invalid integer suggests checking the format. An out-of-range value suggests choosing a quantity between the documented limits. A string such as something went wrong would discard information we already have at the point of failure.

Represent those cases with an enum. The enum is a compact vocabulary shared by the parser, tests and interface. Start with the cases that have a real use. A huge error hierarchy invented before you have callers can make a small programme harder to follow. Conversely, if the caller needs to distinguish two failures, collapsing them into one generic category makes the next layer guess. The right level of detail comes from the responses the application actually supports.

sections.heading: Write the parser as a sequence of decisions
paragraphs: First trim surrounding whitespace, because our interface deliberately accepts a quantity with spaces around it. Next reject an empty string. Parse the remaining text as `u32`, translating a parse failure into our public error category. Finally enforce the range and return the quantity. The order matters: it tells us which error an input should receive. Document that extremely large decimal input may fail parsing before it reaches the range check, because it does not fit into `u32`.

This sequence is easy to trace by hand. For a blank string, stop at Empty. For twelve written as letters, stop at InvalidInteger. For zero, parsing succeeds but the range check fails. For seven, every stage succeeds. Do that trace before adding more code. A parser that you can explain through four small inputs gives you a reliable foundation for a user-facing message and a test suite.

sections.heading: The question mark propagates a failure
paragraphs: In the parser, `?` unwraps the successful parsed value or returns the error from the current function. It is an early return on the error path, not a retry and not a panic. Our `map_err` changes the parser's library error into the application category before propagation. That conversion is a conscious choice: this small interface needs to identify an invalid integer, while detailed parse internals would not change the user's next action.

In a larger system, preserving the underlying error may be important for diagnosis. Decide that from the needs of the next layer rather than automatically replacing every error with a sentence. A concise `?` can make a sequence of fallible operations readable, but it cannot decide what context the caller will need. Read a chain of question marks as a series of exit points and ask what information travels along each exit.

image.alt: Result branches into Ok(value), which continues, and Err(error), which returns to the caller through the question mark operator.
image.caption: The diagram shows propagation from the current function. The caller chooses whether to show, retry, skip or stop.

sources.title: Propagating errors in the Rust Book

sections.heading: Handle the result at the interface boundary
paragraphs: The part of the programme talking to a person should turn an error into a response. Use `match` to display a clear message for each quantity error. The successful path can create the workshop order. The parser remains reusable because it does not decide whether output belongs in a terminal, a sheet, a form or a test. Separating parsing from presentation also keeps its tests small and predictable.

Write messages that help someone correct the input. Enter a quantity gives a next step. Use a whole number identifies the required format. Choose a quantity from one to one hundred communicates the accepted range. Do not copy an entire stack of internal details into the normal interface just because you have them. Keep useful diagnostic information available for development, while giving the user a response suited to the task they are trying to complete.

sections.heading: Add context without losing the original cause
paragraphs: Imagine importing twenty workshop orders from a file. InvalidInteger now needs context: which row contained the invalid quantity? Add that information at the layer that knows about rows, rather than teaching the basic quantity parser about files. The low-level function can still report the quantity error, while the import layer attaches a row number. This preserves reuse and makes the report actionable for the person fixing the file.

For systems errors, an error chain can retain an underlying cause while adding the operation that failed. The standard `Error` trait supports reporting a source error, and `Display` supplies a readable representation. Our small enum does not need that machinery to demonstrate the idea, but larger application boundaries may benefit from it. The important design question is whether a caller can understand both the failed operation and the reason, without reverse-engineering a generic message.

sections.heading: Choose panic for a different kind of failure
paragraphs: Expected invalid input should normally travel through a result the caller can handle. A panic has a different role: it can signal a violated assumption or an unrecoverable situation in the selected programme design. `unwrap` and `expect` panic when their expected success is absent. They can be useful in tightly controlled examples or tests, but using them on arbitrary user input turns an ordinary correction into abrupt failure.

Ask what the interface promises before choosing a response. If the workshop app accepts text entered by a person, malformed text is foreseeable. If a test constructs a value that must be valid for the test itself to make sense, a failed expectation can clearly identify a broken setup. Write the invariant beside that expectation. Avoid calling every unexpected value a programmer error when it actually arrived through an external boundary you have not validated.

sections.heading: Test the contract at its boundaries
paragraphs: Turn the earlier hand traces into tests. Check empty input, invalid text, zero, the lowest accepted value, the highest accepted value and the first value above it. Add surrounding whitespace because accepting it was a deliberate part of the parser contract. Check a value too large for `u32` so the parse-versus-range distinction remains documented. These cases protect decisions a user can observe, rather than simply repeating the function's internal lines.

Test error categories as values. Comparing an enum is usually less fragile than comparing a complete English message, whose wording you may improve later. Then add a small interface check for the messages you actually show. Keep both questions visible: did the parser classify the failure correctly, and did the interface help the user? A successful test run is persuasive when you can explain the behaviours it covers and the behaviours still outside its scope.

sections.heading: Avoid accidental disclosure in diagnostics
paragraphs: Error context is useful, but more detail is not automatically better. A failed file operation might involve a private path; a failed request might include a token; a rejected record might contain personal information. Decide which context belongs in ordinary output, which belongs in restricted diagnostic output, and which should not be retained at all. Design that decision alongside the error type instead of adding indiscriminate logging after a failure appears.

For our workshop example, a row number and a category usually help without reproducing the entire order. During local development, you can examine a controlled fixture to investigate a bug. For a deployed product, avoid treating arbitrary user content as a harmless diagnostic string. This is an application design concern, not a capability `Result` supplies automatically. The type makes failure explicit; you still choose a responsible and useful way to present it.

sections.heading: Practise a failure story from input to response
paragraphs: Copy the parser into a small project, add the display function, and call it with each fixture. Predict the result before running it. Then change the accepted range and update the contract tests. Add a rule that the quantity must be even, with its own named error. Decide where that check belongs in the sequence and which error an out-of-range odd number should receive. Your answer should follow a documented rule rather than accidental branch order.

Finish by explaining one failure end to end: the original input, the validation step that rejected it, the error value returned, the layer that handled it, and the message the person received. Then explain one successful path with the same precision. When both stories are clear, you have designed more than a parser that compiles. You have a reusable boundary whose outcomes the next part of the programme can trust, test and communicate.

title: What it means to run a real Rust compiler on an iPhone
summary: Follow a source file through local compilation, diagnostics, WASI execution, dependency preparation, and the practical limits of a phone-sized Rust workspace.

sections.heading: A compiler, not a remote text checker
paragraphs: The useful question is not whether an editor can color Rust syntax. It is whether a change to your program reaches a compiler that checks the same kinds of rules you would meet in a real project. Crabrix bundles a pinned Rust compiler and its wasm32-wasip1 sysroot inside the iOS app. When you press Check, that compiler parses your source, resolves names and types, and applies borrow checking on the device. The Problems view is fed by compiler diagnostics, not by a fixed set of quiz answers or a remote service pretending to understand the code.

That distinction changes how you learn. If you move a String into a function and use it again, the error comes from the language rules your own project must obey. If you misspell a variable, the highlighted span refers to your file. Fixing the program means changing the source and asking the compiler again. Crabrix still has to present the feedback clearly, but the verdict is produced by a real toolchain. The exact compiler target and toolchain identity are pinned for an app build so behavior can be compared and investigated rather than quietly changing from one session to the next.

sections.heading: From source to a result
paragraphs: There are four distinct stages in the usual loop. First, an editable source file lives in the project workspace. Second, the local compiler checks it and, for a requested build, produces a WASI binary. Third, Crabrix executes that binary in a fresh runtime store. Fourth, the program writes output or returns a result that the app shows in Output. The compiler can also report diagnostics along the way. A failed check stops before a new program can run; an empty Output panel after a successful build may simply mean the program never printed anything.

Keeping those stages separate helps with debugging. A red diagnostic is about code the compiler could not accept. A panic or nonzero exit after a successful build is about a program that did run. A line from println! belongs to stdout, not to the compiler. When you modify a file, predict which stage your change can affect before tapping Run. If a formatting placeholder is wrong, expect a compile-time message. If a branch prints only for one input, expect the build to succeed and output to vary with the input.

image.alt: Infographic showing source file, local Rust compiler, WASI binary, and local output inside an on-device boundary, with diagnostics branching from the compiler.
image.caption: The app keeps compilation and program execution as separate, observable steps.

sections.heading: What “local” does and does not promise
paragraphs: The compiler and runtime execute on the device. Source does not need to be uploaded to a compilation server for Check or Run. The app bundle contains the pinned compiler and sysroot; a phone does not download new compiler executable code to replace them. This is a concrete statement about the build loop, not a claim that every app feature is offline or that network access never occurs. Course downloads, a supported dependency that has not been cached, or importing a project can involve the network. A cached and pinned package archive can be reused for an offline rebuild under the conditions documented in the app.

A project terminal is likewise local but deliberately narrower than a Mac shell. It offers commands over the project workspace; it does not start arbitrary host processes or grant a Rust program unrestricted iOS access. The WASI guest has no network import. These limits protect the boundary between a user-edited project and the host app. They also matter when evaluating a crate: code that expects a native C library, an executable build script, or a socket opened by the guest cannot be assumed to work simply because it compiles on a desktop.

sections.heading: Why WebAssembly and WASI appear in the design
paragraphs: Rust normally compiles native code for a target platform. In Crabrix, the bundled compiler is itself a WebAssembly program run through CrabrixRuntime, a Swift interpreter derived from WasmKit. The project output targets wasm32-wasip1. That target gives a defined set of filesystem and process-style interfaces that the app can provide inside a bounded workspace. The runtime can meter execution, limit memory and output, and start a fresh store for program runs. This architecture is different from handing user source to a server or trying to execute an arbitrary new iOS binary.

The target is a compatibility choice, not a promise that every Rust ecosystem package will work. A pure Rust library that fits the supported target and build flow may be usable. A dependency that needs a host executable build.rs or a procedural macro requires capabilities outside the current local subset. The most honest workflow is to check a dependency before a long build, read the compatibility result, and keep an alternative design in mind. Often a small hand-written parser or a crate without native components is enough for a learning project.

sections.heading: The cost of genuine work
paragraphs: A real compiler performs genuine work, and a phone is not a desktop workstation. The first check of a changed project may spend time parsing, resolving packages, checking types, and generating code. Dependencies add more work. Repeating an identical build can benefit from local artifact caches, while changing source or configuration can invalidate some cached results. A spinner is not proof that the app is doing useful work by itself; a trustworthy interface should show which phase is active and surface errors when work stops.

For your own experiments, compare the right things. Run a tiny one-file program once, then run it again unchanged, then change one line and run again. Notice which run is fastest and which needs compilation. Avoid extrapolating from one warm cache measurement to a new Cargo project with dependencies. Limits on memory, writable files, runtime, and output can stop an overlarge guest. Treat those boundaries as part of the supported environment, just as a desktop toolchain has a target triple and system libraries that define its behavior.

sections.heading: Dependencies: useful, but selective
paragraphs: Cargo makes Rust projects larger than a single source file, and Crabrix supports a focused subset of that workflow. The app can resolve supported crates.io packages, verify downloaded archives against registry checksums, write a lockfile, and build suitable dependencies for its target. Once the exact verified source archives are cached or pinned for offline use, the same packages can be available without another download. That is a useful bridge from a tutorial snippet to a multi-file project with a manifest.

The subset has edges. Procedural-macro crates, executable build scripts, and native C linking are outside the supported local Cargo path. A package may depend on one of these indirectly, so read the whole dependency result rather than just the top-level crate name. A lockfile records a selected dependency graph, but it is not a magic guarantee that every dependency can be compiled for every target. Start with a small pure-Rust dependency, verify it works, then add one package at a time. That makes an incompatibility diagnosable instead of leaving you with a large unresolved graph.

sections.heading: A bounded workspace is a useful workspace
paragraphs: An editable project deserves to survive beyond the lesson that created it. Crabrix keeps project files in a local workspace, with a file tree, source editor, diagnostics, Output, and a project terminal. The terminal can help inspect files or run supported project commands, but it is not an unrestricted shell. That distinction is visible in the product because an honest tool should not imply that it can do what the platform and sandbox do not permit.

The runtime also protects itself from guest behavior. A program can loop forever, produce huge output, or request too much memory. Metering, deadlines, and output bounds give the app ways to stop or contain those cases. Stopping a guest is not the same as proving its algorithm correct; it is a resource policy that keeps the device responsive. When a build or run is interrupted, look at which phase stopped and whether a new binary was produced. Do not interpret an old Output line as the result of the latest failed build.

image.caption: The project workspace is editable while the guest runtime stays inside explicit limits.

sections.heading: Read a diagnostic as evidence
paragraphs: Rust diagnostics often contain a primary message, a source span, notes, and sometimes a suggested change. Begin with the first meaningful error, not the last line in the panel. A missing brace can create many follow-up messages, so repair one cause and check again. If the compiler says “expected X, found Y,” identify which expression produced Y and which function or branch demanded X. This turns the error from a verdict into a map of the program you actually wrote.

For ownership errors, draw the flow of one value: creation, move, borrow, last use. A suggestion to clone may make code compile but can hide an unnecessary allocation or an unclear API. Ask whether a function needs ownership or only a read-only borrow. For a formatting error, count placeholders and supplied values. For a missing trait, inspect the operation that requires it. Each fix should be a conscious statement about the program, not a sequence of edits that happen to quiet the compiler.

sections.heading: A ten-minute experiment
paragraphs: Create a small project and write a function that returns a greeting. First compile and run the program unchanged, and record the exact output. Next misspell a binding name and press Check. Find the highlighted span, predict the smallest correction, then fix it. After that, add a second placeholder to println! but no second argument. Notice that this problem is caught before a new run. Finally restore a valid format and change the text the program prints. You have now observed source editing, compiler validation, a diagnostic, and runtime output as separate events.

Repeat the same method with a borrowed String: let a helper accept &str, call it with a String, and use the String afterward. Then change the helper to take ownership and compare the compiler response. This is more instructive than memorizing a slogan about borrowing. Keep a short note of each prediction, the actual evidence, and the rule you inferred. A local compiler is most valuable when it becomes a tool for testing your understanding, not just a button you press until the red text disappears.

sections.heading: Where to continue
paragraphs: The free Learn section on this website provides the same course topics and examples to read without an account. Start with Rust Basics if you are new to the language, then move through ownership and project structure before tackling concurrency or unsafe code. On the device, open an example in Code and make a durable project copy so you can experiment beyond the lesson. When a project grows, check the target and dependency limits before assuming desktop Cargo behavior.

Crabrix is a focused local Rust workspace. Its strength is that the edit, check, run, and inspect cycle can happen where you are, with a compiler whose identity and limits are visible. Its limits are part of that story. The fastest way to learn is to make a precise prediction, change one thing, read the evidence, and repeat.

title: From a Rust lesson to a project you own
summary: A practical path from reading one example to predicting behavior, editing source, handling errors, and keeping an independent Rust project.

sections.heading: Reading is a starting point
paragraphs: A short example can make a concept look obvious while someone else has already made every choice. You see a finished function, a correct type, and a successful output. The real skill starts when one detail changes: an input is empty, a value moves, or a branch returns the wrong type. Crabrix lessons are meant to give you an idea and a concrete Rust snippet, but the way to make that idea yours is to predict, edit, and check it. The compiler then tests a claim about your own code instead of asking you to remember someone else’s answer.

The Academy currently organizes six Rust courses with 142 guided lessons, plus Algorithm Atlas with 200 patterns across 600 steps. Those counts describe the catalog, not a promise that reading every page automatically makes someone fluent. A useful lesson has to make the next action clear: what to notice, what to change, what result to expect, and how to explain a surprise. On the website every lesson is open to read. In the app you can take an example into the editor and turn it into a project that remains yours.

sections.heading: The four-step learning loop
paragraphs: Begin by reading the example slowly enough to name each value and the operation that uses it. Before running anything, write down the output or the compiler error you expect. Then change one line and ask the same question again. Only after you have a prediction should you press Check or Run. Compare the evidence with your prediction, and revise your mental model if they differ. This order matters: without a prediction, even a surprising result is easy to accept without understanding.

For a tiny greeting, the prediction may be one exact line of stdout. For a borrow, predict whether the caller can still use the owned String after a function call. For a match, list every variant and which arm handles it. A failed prediction is useful when you can point to the rule you misunderstood. Keep the experiment small enough that one changed line has one plausible effect. If you change types, branches, and formatting all at once, the next diagnostic may tell you little about which idea was wrong.

image.alt: Infographic of the learning loop: read, predict, edit, check or run, and repeat.
image.caption: A prediction turns compiler feedback into an explanation you can test.

sections.heading: Copy the lesson into an independent project
paragraphs: In the iOS app, opening lesson source in Code creates an editable project copy. The project is separate from the downloaded course material. This is an important ownership boundary for the learner: you can make mistakes, rename files, or delete code without corrupting the lesson you may want to reread. You can also return to My Projects later rather than losing the experiment when you leave the lesson. The first copied version is only a starting point; the value lies in what you do to it.

Give the project a question. Instead of “I am practicing Rust,” try “What changes when this function borrows a String rather than taking it?” or “What should an empty list return?” Put that question in a note or comment, change the smallest relevant piece of code, and check. If the compiler rejects your experiment, read its message before undoing the change. If it succeeds, run an input that distinguishes your new behavior from the old one. A project becomes durable learning material when it records a sequence of understood decisions.

sections.heading: A concrete first experiment
paragraphs: Start with a list of names and a loop that prints a greeting for each one. Borrow the list during iteration so the list still exists afterward. Predict the output for two names, including punctuation and line breaks, then run it. Add a third name and predict again. This seems elementary, but it establishes the habit of separating collection contents, iteration, formatting, and output into distinct parts you can reason about.

Now remove the reference from the loop and try to use the list afterward. The compiler may tell you that the vector was moved by the iteration. Read the diagnostic as evidence about ownership: the loop took values rather than merely borrowing them. Restore the reference and explain why the later use works. Next try an empty vector. The loop runs zero times, so there is no greeting. Decide whether that is acceptable or whether your program should print an explicit “no names” message. You have moved from copying syntax to defining behavior for a boundary case.

sections.heading: Make compiler errors part of the plan
paragraphs: An error is most useful when you created it on purpose. Change `&names` to `names` in the loop, predict whether `names.len()` remains legal, and press Check. Identify the line where ownership moved and the later line that tried to use the old binding. Do not immediately add `.clone()` merely to remove the error. Cloning can be correct when independent owned copies are needed, but in this example a borrow expresses the intent more clearly and avoids copying elements.

Try a different controlled mistake: give a function an `i32` argument where it expects `&str`. The diagnostic compares the actual and expected types. Ask whether the caller should convert its value, or whether the function signature is wrong for your intended API. That question is more valuable than a mechanical cast. Fix one error, compile again, and only then inspect the next. Compiler messages often cascade from one missing delimiter or type mismatch, so treating every line as an independent bug wastes time.

sections.heading: Handle the first real input
paragraphs: A copied example often contains only known-good values. A real project eventually reads text it did not choose. Parsing is the first useful boundary to add. Accept a text number, call `parse::<i32>()`, and handle both `Ok(number)` and `Err(error)`. Decide what the user should see when the input is empty, contains letters, or exceeds the number type’s range. This is where a tutorial becomes software: you must define behavior for the cases the original snippet did not show.

Keep the failure path recoverable. An `unwrap()` may be fine in a five-line controlled demonstration, but it turns ordinary bad input into a panic. Returning `Result` from a helper lets its caller decide whether to retry, show a message, or stop. Add a test or a small table of inputs and expected outcomes. If you cannot explain why a failed parse is handled one way rather than another, the project needs a clearer requirement. The compiler ensures you handle the type; the product decision is still yours.

sections.heading: Grow the file tree deliberately
paragraphs: One file is enough for a first experiment. Split code into modules when a boundary is clear, not merely because the file reached a certain line count. A parser module can own conversion and error messages; a model module can define the values the rest of the project uses; main can connect input to output. If a function is useful from another module, decide whether to expose it with `pub`. Keep internal helpers private. This gives names to responsibilities while keeping the public API small.

The project workspace supports multiple files and a manifest. Some projects can add supported crates.io dependencies, but check target compatibility before building a design around one. A dependency may transitively require a build script, procedural macro, or native linker that the local target does not support. Start with a small pure-Rust dependency and verify it before adding more. The moment you add files or packages, keep a working version of the project so you can distinguish a module-path error from a dependency problem.

image.alt: An illustrated lesson page becoming a separate project folder with editable source files.
image.caption: The lesson stays a reference; the editable project becomes the place for your experiments.

sections.heading: Use tests for claims you want to keep
paragraphs: A print statement answers “what happened in this run?” A test can preserve a claim for future changes. For a greeting function, test a normal name and an empty name. For parsing, test valid, invalid, and boundary inputs. Name the test after the behavior it protects rather than the method it calls. A test that merely repeats implementation details can pass even while the user-facing result is wrong. Keep expected values visible and specific.

Choose the smallest useful test. A pure function can be tested without invoking the entire app. An integration-style test can check that several modules work together. A manual run is still useful for terminal output and interaction, but it should not be the only guard for a rule you plan to rely on. After changing a function, run the relevant tests and then check the project again. If a test fails, decide whether the behavior or the expectation should change; do not update expected output automatically without understanding the difference.

sections.heading: Debug with a hypothesis
paragraphs: When a program produces the wrong answer, start with one hypothesis that could explain it. “The empty input takes the normal branch” is testable; “Rust is behaving strangely” is not. Inspect the value just before the branch, or add a narrow temporary debug print. Compare it with the value you predicted. If the hypothesis fails, remove that observation and choose another. This is faster than scattering prints across every line and trying to read an ocean of logs afterward.

Separate build errors from runtime behavior. Problems contains compiler diagnostics from code that could not be accepted. Output is where a built program’s stdout and run outcome appear. The project terminal offers supported commands over the workspace, not an unrestricted host shell. Use the tool that answers your current question. If a run was interrupted, confirm whether the visible output belongs to the latest build or an earlier one. Write a regression test after you understand the bug so the same boundary stays covered.

sections.heading: Keep the result and choose the next question
paragraphs: A project copy is useful because it remains editable after the lesson ends. Rename it to describe the experiment, keep the source and tests that explain its behavior, and export it when you want to move it elsewhere. A downloaded course can be updated independently of that project. Offline reading and offline building also differ: a course can be stored on the phone while an exercise using an uncached dependency may still require preparation. Plan accordingly before a trip or a class without connectivity.

One good learning session is not measured by the number of lessons completed. It is measured by a rule you can now explain and a program whose behavior you can predict. After Rust Basics, try ownership with a deliberate move and borrow; after that, build a small multi-file program with one recoverable error. Return to the free web lesson when you need the reference, then use the local compiler to test the next claim. Over time, your project collection becomes evidence of what you can actually make.
